Consistent hashing: each instance gets K virtual nodes on a hash ring (K=100-200 typical); request routes to the next clockwise node from hash(request_key). Consistent hashing (uniform keys): ~33/34/33 split regardless of request duration — if B's requests take 10x longer, B still gets 34 and its queue grows unbounded. Least-connections: as B's in-flight count rises above A/C, new requests route to the faster instances; steady-state distribution inversely proportional to mean service time — if B is 10x slower, it gets ~1/12 of traffic (~8) vs A and C getting ~46 each. Scaling: consistent hashing scales by adding virtual nodes (no coordination needed); least-connections needs the LB to see all instances' load (single global view or gossip), which becomes a bottleneck at >100 instances.

(2) Both sides compute shared secret Z = ECDHE(client_priv, server_pub). (3) HKDF extracts/expandes Z into the master secret, then derives handshake traffic secrets and finally the application traffic secrets — all one-way via HKDF-Expand-Label with distinct labels so no key is ever reused across phases. Forward secrecy comes entirely from the ephemeral ECDHE keys: they exist only in memory for the duration of the handshake and are discarded. After session termination, even if the server's *long-term* private key (used to sign the CertificateVerify message) is later compromised, an attacker cannot derive Z because that requires the client's ephemeral private key, which was never transmitted and no longer exists. Contrast with TLS 1.2 using RSA key transport: the premaster secret is encrypted with the server's long-term public key — a later key compromise lets you decrypt every previously captured session (GnuTLS/NSA-style bulk decryption).
